name: Undo the last thing (a change journal with inverses)
description: A parent can say 'undo that' after Happy adds the wrong reminder, list item, calendar entry or household fact, and Happy reverses its own last write after showing what it will reverse. The 9 Oct audit digest (G006) only reports what happened; nothing in either catalog takes a write back.
example: Jordan texts: 'Undo that, I meant Thursday, not Tuesday.'
how:
OpenClaw has no undo for tool effects. The only rewind found in the installed docs is the Control UI's session rewind, an admin-scoped action that moves the transcript back and does not mention reversing what tools did. So this is in-house work. Each in-house write tool (the household store, the Reminders bridge, the calendar-write server, the hook that pins reminders made with the automations tool) writes a journal row from inside the tool, where the before-state is known: who asked, when, which tool, and the inverse call. The after_tool_call hook only observes results and cannot supply the before-state. An undo_last tool on

-main, limited by a before_tool_call hook to the requester's own rows from the last 24 hours, shows the row, waits for a yes, then runs the inverse: restore the old value or delete the new row, un-complete or delete the reminder item, delete the calendar event Happy created, or 'openclaw automations remove' for a scheduled reminder. A saved note is undone by editing the line in MEMORY.md (F041); derived memory is an operator job with 'openclaw memory forget'. Every write reply ends by saying whether it can be undone.
depends_on: G006 audit digest (can share the journal table)
caveats: Sent things cannot be recalled: a text to the other parent, an email to the owner, a print job, a Sonos announcement. The reply has to say so at the time of sending.

Only Happy's own writes are covered. If a parent has since edited the same reminder or event on a phone, the inverse could overwrite that edit, so the tool should refuse when the item changed after Happy wrote it.
'openclaw memory forget' deletes at once with no confirmation unless --dry-run is passed, and it keeps the source transcripts; it is not something to hand to a chat command.
The phone already has undo for what a person does by hand. This covers only what Happy did on their behalf.

The 9 Oct Reminders bridge (F030) was specified as list, add and complete with no delete. Undo needs a delete, so that delete must accept only item ids that Happy's own journal recorded as created by Happy, enforced inside the tool and not left to the model.

The entry's own example ('I meant Thursday, not Tuesday') is a correction, which the same write tool already handles with a second write. The journal earns its place for overwritten household facts, where the old value would otherwise be gone, and as the audit trail.
safety:
Undo reverses a write that the same person's agent made, so it adds no new reach: no new recipient and no new data source. The hook keys on the requester's handle and blocks on error. It lives on

-main, which does not read untrusted web content, and it cannot touch the other parent's rows.
unverified: That no built-in undo for tool effects exists anywhere in 2026.9.7. This rests on a search of the installed docs for undo, rewind and revert, not on reading the source.
Whether the Reminders command-line tool and the calendar server return stable item ids that an inverse can target; neither is installed yet.
A wider search of the installed docs in this review (undo, revert, checkpoint) also found no undo for tool effects; the dist source was still not read.

Two build facts were missing: the 9 Oct Reminders bridge (F030) was specified with no delete, so undo needs a delete limited to ids in Happy's own journal; and value is lowered because most 'undo' requests, including the entry's own example, are corrections the same write tool already handles.

name: Happy scorecard (personal-agent benchmark themes)
description: A small fixed test set that scores Happy on the ten behaviours OpenClaw's own personal-agent pack checks (reminder round trip, preference recall, no secret echo, stopping after a denied approval, no fake "done", honest partial-failure reports), run against the eval clones after each change. The shipped pack itself cannot run on this install.
example: Tony runs `happy-eval scorecard` after a deploy and reads a ten-line pass or fail table before texting the family that something new is on.
how:
The shipped pack is out of reach: it needs an OpenClaw source checkout and `OPENCLAW_ENABLE_PRIVATE_QA_CLI=1`, drives the synthetic qa-channel with a mock model, and the Homebrew npm install has no qa directory. Build instead: write the ten scenario themes as promptfoo cases in happy-config/evals against the `

-main-eval` clones through promptfoo's `openclaw` provider (the roadmap E0 harness), with fixtures standing in for reminders and approvals, and store the pass rate next to the smoke results. Operator tooling only.
depends_on: F007 and F041, so the reminder and memory cases have something to test
caveats: The upstream pack with a mock model measures the plumbing; a promptfoo port measures the real model and costs tokens on every run.
Ten cases is a regression tripwire, not a benchmark. Anthropic's guidance is to start from 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and to read the transcripts, not only the scores.
Eval clones must keep messaging tools denied, or a reminder test texts the family.
The docs say not to point the upstream pack at live chat services or real accounts.

Several of the ten themes have nothing to exercise on Happy today: no tool is approval-gated, so there is nothing to deny; reminders need F007; preference recall needs F041; thread routing and diagnostics artifacts are developer-surface checks. Start with the themes that apply now (no secret echo, no fake "done", honest partial failure, pending versus done) and add the rest as the tools land.
safety: Runs only against eval clones with fake users and fake secrets; no live channel, no real memory, no accounts.
unverified: That the scenario YAML files are readable in the upstream repository at the 2026.9.7 tag (not fetched).
How promptfoo's tool-trajectory assertions behave against 2026.9.7 (an open item in the roadmap).

name: Overnight interest brief on the research agent
description: ChatGPT Pulse writes five to ten personalised cards overnight, and Gemini scheduled actions do daily topic tracking. Happy's version: each parent keeps a short topic list (town recreation sign-ups, a team, a hobby) and gets at most three sourced lines per topic in the morning, or nothing when there is no news.
example: Trigger: 06:30 job. Tony receives: 'Rec dept: spring soccer registration opens Monday (link, fetched 06:31).'
how: One `automations` job per parent owned by the stateless `research` agent: isolated session, tools limited to `web_search,web_fetch`, announce delivery pinned to that parent. Topics are literal text in the job message, rendered by gen-family from an `interests` list in family.json5, never read from memory. Output follows the F022 citation rule and the job returns `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. 'More of this' or 'drop that topic' is a proposal the parent confirms; the jobs registry (G003) regenerates the job. Seen links are kept in the job's condition-trigger state (`--trigger-script`, compared against `trigger.state`), the F029 pattern, because an isolated run remembers nothing between mornings; Tony creates these jobs from the CLI.
depends_on: F029 trigger-state pattern for seen links
caveats: Pulse is good because it mixes memory, chat history and connected Gmail and Calendar. That mix is exactly what the trifecta rule forbids here, so Happy's brief is deliberately less personal.
The catalog already removed headlines from the morning brief and dropped the Sunday topic brief; this only fits because it is a separate job on an agent with no private data.
Gemini does this for free with up to 10 scheduled actions. If a parent already uses Gemini, skip this.
Without a seen-links state file it will repeat yesterday's item.
Topics travel to Brave and OpenAI, so keep them non-identifying: no kid names, no school name.

Gemini offers scheduled actions (up to 10 active; Google's page describes behaviour with and without a paid AI plan and says the rollout is gradual). If a parent already uses Gemini or Google Alerts, skip this.
An isolated run remembers nothing from yesterday, so de-duplication has to live in the job's condition-trigger state (the F029 pattern); without it the brief repeats items.
safety: The research agent holds no memory and no accounts; the run contains no private data. Delivery is pinned to one parent by the job, so injected web text can at worst produce a misleading line to that parent. Links are shown with fetch time per F022.
unverified: Pulse's plan availability in October 2026; the source is the September 2025 launch report (Pro plan first). OpenAI's own pages returned 403 in this run.

name: Family week board in the Control UI (pinned native report)
description: One always-current page, reachable from the parents' devices on the tailnet, showing this week's events and drivers, bins night, chores and open reminders. A scheduled job refreshes it, so nobody has to ask.
example: Tony opens the Happy board from a Home Screen icon on Sunday evening; the 18:00 job has already replaced the 'This week' table and the 'Due soon' list.
how:
show_widget with a structured report and pin: true writes a native dashboard report (text, metrics, tables, simple charts, links) onto a session's dashboard in the Control UI. Keep one persistent 'Family board' session per parent on

-main; a recurring automation bound to that session with an explicit tool cap (home_weather,

-calendar__*, home-store__*, show_widget) re-sends the same widget name with fresh data. The scheduled surface is pinned-only, which is what is wanted. On demand, /dashboard in a Control UI chat does the same. View it at the Tailscale Serve URL or as a Home Screen web app.
depends_on: Control UI access for each viewer (the identity decision in OCL-01)
caveats: show_widget is not offered in iMessage runs, so the board cannot be requested or shown by text; the evening brief (F014) remains the pushed version.
A native report is limited to 24 blocks and 8 KB, and a table to 40 rows.

Anyone who can open that session in the Control UI sees the board. For Jordan that means Control UI access, which today carries Gateway-wide operator scopes (see OCL-01), so until per-person sign-in is solved the board is Tony-only. A tablet the kids can see would need its own restricted role and a first-names-only board.
The shared calendar already shows in the phones' own calendar widgets; the board is only worth it once it merges calendar, chores, bins and reminders in one place.
Interactive HTML widgets look better but are the wrong choice on an agent that holds private data.
A custom persistent session keeps its history, so the board session's transcript grows with every refresh and holds calendar text; plan a periodic reset.
safety: Native reports accept no HTML, CSS, scripts, network reads or Gateway calls, so the board has no way to send data anywhere; it is pulled by a family device over Tailscale. HTML widgets are different: allowed CDN libraries run inside the widget and can see its content, so they stay off memory-holding agents. The job carries no web tools, so no untrusted content enters the run, and it sends no message.
unverified: Whether a job created by the config generator (rather than from a Control UI chat) can be bound to a persistent Control UI session with show_widget in its tool cap; the docs describe the surface but not the CLI flags
Whether the native iOS app shows session dashboards or only inline widgets

Whether a registry-generated job that targets --session session:<id> with show_widget in --tools counts as the server-authored scheduled tool policy the widget docs require, and whether that custom session's dashboard is listed in the Control UI; both flags exist but the combination is untested

name: Week sheet on paper as a no-model job
description: Adds one thing to F080: the Sunday fridge sheet produced and printed by a plain script on a schedule, with no model call, so there is nothing to inject and nothing to pay for. It is also the fallback when the kitchen screen (HOM-10) is not worth keeping alive.
example: Trigger: Sunday 18:00, one page comes out of the printer.
how: An automation with a command payload (--command-argv) runs a script from the config repo on the Gateway host. The script reads the family home-store and the calendar export, renders one letter-size PDF page and sends it with lp to the named queue, one copy, one-sided, then prints only NO_REPLY so no chat message is sent. The printer queue is added once as in F080. Failures surface through the job's failure alert.
depends_on: a calendar source a host script can read without an agent (for example a shared family calendar export), settled together with F009
caveats: Command payloads run inside the Gateway process as an admin-authored job, outside the sandbox and outside agent tool policy; the script must be reviewed like any other code in the config repo.
The house printer is a photo inkjet, so a weekly plain-paper page is fine but daily printing is wasteful.
Every phone in the house can already print a PDF itself; the gain is only that the sheet appears without anyone asking.
The sheet is only as good as the calendar and list data behind it.
Neither the home-store (F031) nor a calendar read (F009) exists yet, so this cannot run before they do.

The script reads calendar data outside the per-person MCP servers, so whatever credential or export it uses is a control-plane secret held by the operator; a shared family calendar keeps personal calendars out of it.
Paper on the fridge is read by guests and sitters: first names and times only, no addresses, no medical or money lines.
safety: No model and no outbound message: the script reads family data and writes paper, so there is nothing to inject into. It runs as trusted code on the host with whatever calendar access it is given, which makes code review and that credential the controls. First names only, as for the kids' weekly card (F075).
unverified: The printer's driverless (AirPrint) behaviour from the Mac mini; Canon's product page could not be fetched in this run and only the sibling model's manual was reachable.
Ink cost per plain-paper page on this printer.

The built-in scheduling tool is listed as `automations`, with `cron` kept as an alias (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:73).

That one job takes exactly one delivery target (hence two jobs or one group chat for two parents); I saw single-target examples only.
Groups are off today, so a family group chat target needs the iMessage group allowlist switched on first.
The home-store checklist, the F007 reminder path and the promptfoo newsletter eval are in-house pieces.
PDF or image newsletters are not read: the IMAP path passes attachment names only.

name: School platform feed map: what each system really sends
description: A per-platform setup recipe so the school mailbox receives one predictable email per platform per day: ParentSquare in Digest mode, and PowerSchool's scheduled grade, attendance and balance emails, which can be sent straight to the school mailbox through PowerSchool's 'Additional Notification Emails' field. Canvas has no verified path here: its API needs a personal token and its observer calendar feed could not be read. It also records what has no feed: urgent ParentSquare alerts bypass the digest and reach phones first, and closings arrive through those alerts, not through any public closings feed.
example: Sunday week-ahead line: 'PowerSchool weekly summary: attendance 5/5 both kids; lunch balance low for one account. ParentSquare digest: picture day Thursday, permission slip due Wednesday.'
how: Per platform, the parent sets notification preferences once: ParentSquare posts to Digest (one evening summary) with email on; PowerSchool Email Notifications to Weekly or Daily with 'Summary of Current Grades and Attendance' and 'Balance Alert' ticked, and the school mailbox address from F051 typed into PowerSchool's 'Additional Notification Emails' field so the report arrives there directly with no forward. For ParentSquare, register the school mailbox as the contact address where the school allows it. Those senders go on the mailbox's `allowedSenders` (through G016), the `school-mail` reader handles each message, and the F056 digest prints the lines. A ParentSquare calendar subscription, or a Canvas calendar feed link if the parent's observer account shows one, is subscribed in the family calendar (G012) rather than parsed. Urgent alerts stay on the parents' phones; F055 is a backup, not the primary path.
depends_on: knowing which platforms the district uses
caveats: ParentSquare says alerts and notices always come through regardless of the digest setting; the phone will beat Happy on closings and lockdown notices every time.
PowerSchool emails carry grades and attendance, which are a child's education records; they go to the cloud model under store:false unless that leg waits for a local model.

Canvas documents an API where an observer can list the observed student's calendar events, but it needs a personal access token, which would be a per-person host-side MCP and is out of scope for the mailbox path.
ClassDojo's help page refused this run's fetch; search snippets suggest app users get push instead of email, which would mean no feed at all for app users.
No national or state school-closings feed was found or verified; the district's own alert is the source.
safety: All school mail is untrusted and is read only by the memory-less `school-mail` agent behind a sender allowlist with verified authentication; that agent has no web or file tools and can only announce to the two parents. Links are relayed only when their domain matches the allowlisted sender (existing F056 rule). No agent logs in to any school portal and no portal credentials are stored.
unverified: ClassDojo notification behaviour (page returned 403).
Canvas's iCal calendar feed for observers (the guide page could not be opened in either run; only the REST API page was read).
Whether PowerSchool lets a parent add an extra recipient address for the scheduled emails (seen in a search summary, not on the fetched page).
Exact sender addresses and authentication results for each platform's email.
How a parent subscribes to the ParentSquare calendar (the page read is a product page for districts and gives no steps).

name: Google Classroom guardian summaries in the school digest
description: Google Classroom can email a guardian a daily or weekly summary of each child's missing work, upcoming work and class activity. Happy reads that summary in the school mailbox and adds one 'missing / due this week' line per kid to the afternoon school digest, with a day-before reminder for anything due.
example: Trigger: the weekday Classroom summary arrives in the school mailbox. The 16:00 digest then carries: '4th grader: 1 missing (reading log); science poster due Thursday.'
how: One-time human step: each teacher (or the school administrator) invites the dedicated school mailbox address (F051) as a guardian and a parent accepts the invitation from that mailbox; Google says summaries can go to any email address. Add Google's Classroom sender to the IMAP account's `allowedSenders` with `senderAuth.min: "verified"` so the summary is admitted like other school mail. The extraction happens inside the existing F056 digest job, not in the per-message IMAP reader, which has no store to hand rows to: the digest job (isolated, `--tools` limited to the read-only school-mail server, home-store and `llm-task`) reads the day's summary, turns it into {kid, missing[], upcoming[]} with `llm-task` and a JSON Schema, and relays titles and dates only, never links. `llm-task` is the only tool the `school-mail` reader holds, as F082 already assigns; it has no memory. Day-before reminders reuse F007.
depends_on: the school uses Google Classroom and the teacher turns guardian summaries on
caveats: Only useful if the kids' classes run on Google Classroom; many elementary schools use other tools. Not checked for this family.
Google's teacher page says class summaries are turned off until the teacher enables them, and the invitation must be accepted within 120 days.
Summaries do not include grades.
Google already sends this email to the parent for free. Happy's added value is merging it into the one digest both parents read and setting the reminder.
If a parent stays the guardian and auto-forwards the summary instead, the forwarded mail may fail the IMAP plugin's sender authentication.
A Google Account is needed to view or change the summary settings (frequency, unsubscribe), even though the summary itself can go to any address.
safety: The reader has no tools and no memory, so school mail (untrusted content) cannot reach private data or a send path. The digest job relays structured fields, not raw text or URLs. Outbound goes only to the two parents through the pinned family delivery primitive. Kid first names and assignment titles reach the cloud model under store:false, the same exposure Tony already accepted for the school mailbox.
unverified: The exact From address or domain Google uses for guardian summaries (needed for allowedSenders).
Whether this family's school uses Google Classroom at all.
Whether one student can have the school mailbox as an extra guardian next to both parents; Google's page implies several guardians but does not state a limit.

name: Study guide photo to practice quiz, run by a parent
description: A parent photographs the study guide or vocabulary sheet and Happy quizzes from it: ten questions, one at a time, hint first, answer key at the end. Alexa+ and Gemini both ship this; the catalog only covers drills from a pasted word list.
example: Jordan sends a photo of the science study guide and texts: 'quiz us on this, 10 questions, one at a time.'
how:
Needs inbound attachments on (`channels.imessage.includeAttachments: true`, F001) behind the F084 document gate. `

-main` reads the photo with the reply model's own vision, and a small workspace skill (see MKT-03) fixes the format: one question per message, wait for the answer, one hint before revealing, score at the end, no web lookups. An optional one-shot `automations` reminder offers a re-quiz the night before the test. No new tool: once attachments and the gate are in place this is a prompt-only addition.
depends_on:
F007 automations tool on

-main (only for the optional re-quiz reminder)
MKT-03 skill (optional; needs the `read` tool, see MKT-03)
caveats: Parent-run only: the kids are not users, and the parent holds the phone. The kid agent stays off the cloud model.
The ChatGPT or Gemini app on a parent's phone does the same thing today; Happy's only edge is that it lives in the same thread and can schedule the re-quiz.
Models write wrong answer keys, especially for arithmetic and for facts the sheet does not state. Tell it to quiz only from what is on the page and spot-check.
A text quiz shows spelling words on screen, so spelling still needs the read-aloud variant in F074.
safety:
The photo is untrusted content read by an agent that holds memory, but `

-main` has no browse tool and can only reply to its owner, so the trifecta is not closed. School worksheets go to the cloud vision model under store:false, which is decision 3 in the catalog. No kid account talks to a cloud model.

name: School lunch menu answers (no documented feed)
description: 'What is for lunch tomorrow?' sounds like an easy monitor, but the product page read for the common menu platform, Nutrislice, describes a website and app for parents and mentions no public API, feed or calendar subscription. The realistic version has no feed at all: the parent sends the month's menu once (PDF or photo), Happy proposes the rows and stores them after a yes, and the evening brief reads tomorrow's row. The lunch-money line comes from PowerSchool's balance email where the district uses it.
example: A parent texts 'what's for lunch Thursday?' and Happy answers from the stored month, or the 19:30 brief adds 'Lunch tomorrow: pasta; pack lunch for the one who hates it.'
how:
Recommended path: the parent forwards the monthly menu PDF or a photo (F001/F002); `

-main` extracts date and entree rows, shows them back for a yes (F011 snap-to-action) and stores them through `home-store__schedule_upsert` (F031); F014 reads tomorrow's row. Balance line: PowerSchool 'Balance Alert' email through the F051 mailbox into F056. Not recommended: a host script calling the menu site's unpublished JSON endpoint. `web_fetch` does not execute JavaScript, so if the district's menu page is script-rendered the research agent cannot read it either.
depends_on: F001 and F002 attachments and PDF understanding
knowing which menu platform the district uses
caveats: The vendor's own app already shows the menu on the parent's phone (its allergen filtering was seen only in search results, not on the page fetched); Happy must never be the allergy authority.
Menus change during the month; a once-a-month import will sometimes be wrong.
An unpublished endpoint can change or be blocked without notice and using it may breach the vendor's terms.
Districts on other platforms (several exist) need their own check.
Calendar-grid menu PDFs and photos are easy to misread; the proposed rows must be confirmed by the parent before they are stored.
safety: The PDF path uses content the parent chose to send and holds it in the family's own store; no browsing is involved. If the experimental script were built it would be a model-free host job, never a tool on a memory-holding agent.
unverified: The unpublished Nutrislice JSON endpoint and its URL pattern (reported by community projects found in search; no vendor documentation was found, so it is not cited).
Whether the family's district uses Nutrislice at all.
Nutrislice's terms on automated access.
That the district's menu site is rendered by script (assumed; if it is plain HTML the research agent could read it).
That Nutrislice offers no feed anywhere (only one product page was read).

The recommended path (parent sends the monthly menu, Happy stores rows after a yes) is an ordinary build on F001, F002 and F031, so readiness is 'build'; only the unpublished-endpoint path is experimental and stays not recommended.

name: Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks
description: A grid of every weekday the kids have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, the ten or so summer weeks) against who covers it: camp, grandparents, a trip, a parent off work. Happy keeps the grid, lists the open cells months ahead, tracks registration dates and forms, and at tax time lists what was paid to which day camp. The existing features report the calendar; none of them plans coverage.
example: Trigger: first Sunday of February. Happy texts both parents: 'Jordan coverage: 4 of 10 weeks open for the 10-year-old, 6 for the 8-year-old. Two camps you saved open registration this week.'
how:
Inputs: the district calendar (a subscribed feed, G012, or a photo or PDF through snap-to-action, F011) gives the no-school weekdays; parents add coverage by text. Store: household store rows (F031) keyed by date range and child nickname, with a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a provider name. Jobs: a monthly isolated job on

-main from January to May, and weekly in the four weeks before each break ('--cron'), listing open cells; page watchers for 'registration opens' on camps the parents name (F029, created by Tony); options research by the stateless research agent given ages, weeks and a distance only (F026). Parents register and pay themselves. After paying, a parent sends the receipt and Happy records amount and provider. In February it lists day-camp totals per provider and which providers still lack a taxpayer number, because IRS Publication 503 treats day camp, and not overnight camp, as a possible work-related care expense for a child under 13, and asks for the provider's name, address and taxpayer number (Form W-10 is the request form).
depends_on: G012 or F011 for the district calendar
F029 watchers and F026 research (need the research agent)
caveats: Most states set the school year near 180 days (28 states in the NCES table), which leaves roughly 80 weekdays a year without school, holidays included. The planner earns its keep only if both parents work on those days.
Camp sites are often script-heavy or bot-walled. Expect 'could not verify' and rely on the parent pasting dates.
Registration is a booking and a payment. Happy stops at the reminder and the link.
The tax list is for the preparer, not tax advice. Whether a camp qualifies depends on facts Happy does not have.
A shared spreadsheet does the grid. The gain here is the reminders and the tie-in to forms and receipts.
safety:
The grid lives with

-main, which holds private data and does not browse. The research agent gets ages, date ranges and distance only, never names, school or address. Watchers run on research with no private data. No registration, booking or payment is performed. Receipts pass the document privacy gate before any cloud call.
unverified: Whether the family's district publishes a calendar feed or only a PDF.
That the 2025 edition of Publication 503 carries over unchanged to the 2026 tax year.

name: Enrolment and camp paperwork kit
description: Every August and every camp season the same documents are asked for again: the immunization record, a recent physical, insurance details, emergency contacts, proof of address. Happy keeps a per-child index of where each document is and when it stops being accepted, warns before a form is due, and prepares the copy-paste answers. The parent fills, signs and submits.
example: Jordan texts: 'Camp forms for both kids are due May 1. What do I still need?'
how: One Markdown page per child in the shared family folder, indexed through memory.search.extraPaths (F043 step 1). For each document it records where the official copy lives (the pediatric office, the state immunization registry, the filing cabinet), the date on it, and the date it stops being accepted. CDC says it holds no vaccination records and points parents to the child's doctor, the state immunization information system and the school, so the page notes which of those worked last time. A dated row per form in the household store (F031) drives the reminders: 'the physical on file is older than this camp accepts, book a visit' and 'forms due in 14 days'. The health-form helper (F067) supplies the copy-paste block. Scans stay in Files or the paper folder; only the index goes to Happy.
caveats: Requirements differ by state, district and camp. Happy tracks what each form asked for last time; it does not know the rules.
The official immunization record has to come from the doctor or the state registry. Happy cannot fetch it, because portal logins are out of scope.
Signing is done by the parent, with the phone's markup tools or on paper. Happy never signs, fills a web form or submits.
An index of where documents are is itself sensitive. Keep ID numbers, policy numbers and certificate numbers out of it.
safety: Index pages hold locations and dates, not the documents or identifiers. They sit in the parents' private agents' search path, nothing is browsed in the same turn, and nothing is sent outside the family. Children's health details stay out of research handoffs.
unverified: Whether this state's immunization registry gives parents direct online access.
Typical validity windows for school and camp physicals; twelve months is often quoted but was not sourced here.
